claims.text: Spark plasma sintering in a controlled environment can produce single-phase ZrB2 below 1700 °C.
SPS below 1700 °C will provide substantial microstructural densification of ZrB2.
SPS will refine or beneficially engineer the grain boundaries of ZrB2.
SPS will generate an in situ surface-passivation layer on ZrB2.
The proposed SPS treatment will improve oxidation durability relative to conventionally processed lower-temperature ZrB2.
The proposed SPS treatment will improve resistance to liquid plating-metal corrosion relative to conventionally processed lower-temperature ZrB2.
The starting high-purity ZrB2 powder has strong Zr–B and B–B bonds.
SPS at approximately 1600–1700 °C, with optimized pressure and dwell time, will produce a dense, fine-grained, passivated ZrB2 microstructure.
The proposed material will remain applicable under oxidizing service conditions up to approximately 1200 °C.
The proposed material will remain applicable during exposure to a liquid plating-metal bath.
Pulsed electric current and applied pressure during SPS activate rapid densification.
Rapid SPS processing limits grain growth and reduces processing time.
The lower thermal budget preserves beneficial microstructural features.
Protective surface layers formed during processing inhibit oxidation.
Protective surface layers deter infiltration by liquid plating metal.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have improved structural integrity compared with both high-temperature single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have mechanical strength comparable to that of high-temperature single-phase ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have reduced oxidation rates and greater liquid-metal corrosion resistance.
Conventional ZrB2 specimens processed near or above 1700 °C retain residual porosity and have inadequate oxidation and corrosion resistance.

contradictions.description: The central claim requires processing below 1700 °C, but the proposed range includes 1700 °C and the boundary is stated as a maximum of 1700 °C.

The experiment specifies only an SPS group and a conventional lower-temperature group, whereas the falsification rule also requires comparison with conventionally high-temperature-produced ZrB2; that required control is not included in the design.
The baseline is called 'lower-temperature processed' while being described as produced near or above 1700 °C, whereas the hypothesis uses below 1700 °C as the defining lower-temperature target.
